title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: On August 30, Pierre reached Moscow. Near the city gates he was met by Count Rostopchin's adjutant.
"We've been looking for you everywhere," said the adjutant. "The count wants to see you urgently. He asks you to come at once on a very important matter."
Without going home, Pierre took a cab and drove to see the Moscow commander in chief.

Count Rostopchin had returned to town from his summer villa at Sokolniki only that morning. The anteroom and reception room of his house were full of officials who had been summoned or had come for instructions. Vasilchikov and Platov had already met with the count and explained that it was impossible to defend Moscow — it would have to be surrendered. Though this news was being kept from the residents, the officials — the heads of the various government departments — knew that Moscow would soon fall to the enemy, just as Rostopchin himself knew it. To avoid personal responsibility, they had all come to the governor to ask how to handle their departments.
As Pierre was entering the reception room, a courier from the army came out of Rostopchin's private room.
In answer to the questions people fired at him, the courier made a despairing gesture with his hand and passed through the room.

While waiting in the reception room, Pierre watched the various officials — old and young, military and civilian — with weary eyes. They all seemed dissatisfied and uneasy. Pierre approached a group of men, one of whom he knew. After greeting Pierre, they continued their conversation.
"If they're sent away and brought back later, no harm done — but as things stand now, nobody can guarantee anything."
"But look at what he writes..." said another, pointing to a printed sheet in his hand.
"That's a different matter. That's meant for the people," said the first.
"What is it?" asked Pierre.
"Oh, another broadsheet."
Pierre took it and began reading.

His Serene Highness has passed through Mozhaysk to join up with the troops moving toward him and has taken up a strong position where the enemy won't attack soon. Forty-eight guns with ammunition have been sent to him from here, and his Serene Highness says he will defend Moscow to the last drop of blood and is even prepared to fight in the streets. Don't worry, brothers — the courts are closed because things need to be put in order, and we'll deal with the criminals our own way! When the time comes I'll call for both townsmen and peasant lads, and I'll raise the cry a day or two beforehand — but they're not needed yet, so I'm holding my tongue. An ax will do nicely, a hunting spear isn't bad, but a three-pronged pitchfork is best of all: a Frenchman is no heavier than a sheaf of rye. Tomorrow after dinner I'll take the Iberian icon of the Mother of God to the wounded at the Catherine Hospital, where we'll bless some water. That will help them get well quicker. I'm well now too — one eye was sore but now I'm keeping watch with both.
"But military men have told me it's impossible to fight in the city," said Pierre, "and that the position..."
"Of course! That's exactly what we were saying," replied the first speaker.
"And what does he mean by 'One eye was sore but now I'm watching with both'?" asked Pierre.

"The count had a sty," the adjutant replied, smiling, "and was very upset when I told him people had been asking what was wrong with him. By the way, Count," he added suddenly, turning to Pierre with a smile, "we hear you have family troubles — that the countess, your wife..."
"I haven't heard anything," Pierre replied indifferently. "But what have you heard?"
"Oh, well, you know how people invent things. I'm only saying what I heard."
"But what did you hear?"
"Well, they say," the adjutant continued with the same smile, "that the countess, your wife, is preparing to go abroad. I'm sure it's nonsense..."
"Possibly," Pierre remarked, looking around absently. "And who is that?" he asked, indicating a short old man in a clean blue peasant coat, with a big snow-white beard and eyebrows and a ruddy face.
"Him? That's a tradesman — the restaurant keeper, Vereshchagin. Maybe you've heard about that business with the proclamation."
"Oh, so that's Vereshchagin!" said Pierre, studying the firm, calm face of the old man and looking for any sign that he might be a traitor.
"That's not the man himself — that's the father of the one who wrote the proclamation," said the adjutant. "The young man is in prison, and I expect things will go badly for him."
An old gentleman wearing a decoration and another official, a German with a cross around his neck, approached the speaker.

"It's a complicated story, you know," said the adjutant. "That proclamation appeared about two months ago. The count was informed and ordered an investigation. Gabriel Ivanovich here made the inquiries. The proclamation had passed through exactly sixty-three hands. He'd ask one person, 'Where did you get it?' — 'From so-and-so.' He'd go to the next — 'Where did you get it?' — and so on until he reached Vereshchagin, a half-educated tradesman, 'a pet of a merchant,' as they say." The adjutant smiled. "They asked him, 'Who gave it to you?' Now the point is, we knew who'd given it to him. He could only have gotten it from the Postmaster. But evidently they'd made some arrangement. He answered: 'From nobody — I wrote it myself.' They threatened and questioned him, but he stuck to his story: 'I wrote it myself.' And so it was reported to the count, who sent for the man. 'Where did you get the proclamation?' — 'I wrote it myself.' Well, you know the count," the adjutant said cheerfully, smiling with pride, "he flew into a terrible rage — just imagine the man's audacity, lying and stubbornness!"
"And the count wanted him to say it came from Klyucharev? I see!" said Pierre.

"Not at all!" the adjutant replied in dismay. "Klyucharev had his own sins to answer for, which is why he was banished. But the point is, the count was furious. 'How could you have written it yourself?' he said, and he grabbed the Hamburg Gazette lying on the table. 'Here it is! You didn't write it — you translated it, and translated it wretchedly, because you don't even know French, you fool!' And what do you think? 'No,' says the man, 'I haven't read any newspapers — I made it up myself.' 'If that's so, you're a traitor and I'll have you tried and hanged! Tell me who gave it to you.' 'I haven't seen any papers — I made it up myself.' And that was the end of it. The count had the father brought in, but the son stuck to his story. He was sent to trial and sentenced to hard labor, I believe. Now the father has come to plead for him. But he's a worthless fellow! You know the type — a tradesman's son, a dandy and ladies' man. He attended some lectures somewhere and thinks the devil himself is no match for him. That's the kind of fellow he is. His father runs a cookshop here by the Stone Bridge, and you know there was a large icon of God Almighty painted with a scepter in one hand and an orb in the other. Well, he took that icon home for a few days, and what did he do? He found some scoundrel of a painter..."
